subtopic: LEVY SYSTEM-STATEMENT ON RESULTS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH BRITAIN
LEVY SYSTEM-STATEMENT ON RESULTS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a first glance at the statement one must come to the conclusion that the ramifications of Britain's entry into the European Common Market will be very great. Thus it would seem logical that there should be a great deal of consultation between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom in which all sectors of the Canadian economy must be involved. Those concerned with agricultural products, as well as those concerned with other commodities, must be given full information at all times. Certainly one would want to have the views of the opposition parties in the House. To this end I suggest that an item in the estimates might be brought before the House in order that this matter may be fully debated and members of the opposition may have an opportunity to put forward their views. This should be done so that, without any intention of hindering Britain in its efforts, Canadians may fully appreciate some of the problems facing that country and so that we may have the opportunity to present our views as to the approach we think should be taken by Canada.
I note that, according to a survey taken in Britain, approximately 70 per cent of the people there are not interested in Britain entering the European Common Market at the moment. This percentage may change as a result of negotiation. In view of the fact that we are willing to co-operate with Great Britain by relaxing some of our existing agreements in order to facilitate her negotiations, I hope Britain will be mindful of our position. Should she become a partner in the European Common Market, I hope her influence will be such that some of the existing barriers to trade will be broken down. I refer particularly to the use of subsidies by European Common Market countries, some of which are greater than the total price we receive for our products at the moment.
Without making further comment, I hope that the government will provide additional information later and
give hon. members the fullest opportunity to explore the possible ramifications of this latest move.

subtopic: LEVY SYSTEM-STATEMENT ON RESULTS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that the whole trade picture for grain is still going to be kept under review, that there is a possibility of returning to the tariff system from the levy system, and that negotiations may continue simply underwrites the uncertainty that we face in this very important area of trade. This flows directly from the failure of the Kennedy Round and the GATT negotiations to reach a satisfactory agreement with the Common Market on trade in farm products, cereal grains in particular. This is the fundamental point. Britain is merely adjusting to these circumstances. We are trying to adjust our trade to what Britain is doing.
The volume of our wheat sales to England has declined steadily in recent years. We have no assurance from the minister that this trend will not continue. We have no assurance from him that as a result of these lengthy negotiations we can be sure of an open entry to the British market and of not only maintaining our present trade in grain but increasing it.
It is time that the government made a clear statement to the House as to the position we are going to occupy with regard to cereal grains and whether we can expect to maintain our present volume of exports to England and to the Common Market. I wonder whether the government has explored the possibility of an associate status for Canada or are we going to find ourselves increasingly shut out of the Common Market? Are we going to lose access to that important market on an increasing scale?
The government should clarify its policy on this matter and also clarify how we are going to maintain our markets. We want answers. The report on the negotiations which the minister has just made to the House does not answer these very important questions.

subtopic: LEVY SYSTEM-STATEMENT ON RESULTS OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also believe that more information should be given to the House when there are changes in the field of exports or imports. We are convinced, however, that agriculture remains the basis of the economic structure of any society, including ours.
We must admit that the economic situation is changing around the world. With regard to exports and imports, we have noted that, for several years now, India and other countries, who sued to purchase part of our wheat production, have become exporting countries.
We understand that circumstances change, and that we must adapt to them, but nevertheless the minister in charge of wheat or grain sales to other countries should always keep the House well informed of the situation facing our wheat and grain producers.
I urge the minister to keep us in future more promptly informed of such matters than he does at present.
In any case, we hope our trade with England and other countries increases in such a way as to permit us adequately to promote Canadian agriculture.

March 17, 1971

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I move
That Bill C-180, respecting the packaging, labelling, sale, importation and advertising of prepackaged and certain other products, be amended by deleting clause 19 thereof and substituting therefor:
"19. A copy of each regulation or amendment to a regulation that the Governor in Council proposes to make under section 11 or 18 shall be published in the Canada Gazette, and in at least one leading news publication in each province not less than once and a reasonable opportunity shall be afforded thereafter to consumers, dealers and other interested persons to make representations with respect thereto."
The purpose of this amendment, Mr. Speaker, is to ensure that the regulations which the minister will have power to set up under the terms of this bill will receive the widest possible dissemination across the country and that consumer groups, individual consumers, manufacturers and small businessmen will have an opportunity before the regulations are officially promulgated to make their views known to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the government.
Under clause 19 of the bill as it is now worded, all the minister has to do after the regulations have been set up

March 17, 1971
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act
is to have them published in the Canada Gazette. Clause 19 reads:
A copy of each regulation or amendment to a regulation that the Governor in Council proposes to make under section 11 or 18 shall be published in the Canada Gazette and a reasonable opportunity shall be afforded to consumers, dealers and other interested persons to make representations with respect thereto.
During the examination of this bill in committee, we heard evidence from most of the witnesses who appeared. Many of them were apprehensive about the legislation because of the wide discretionary powers that the bill gives to the minister. They were concerned that the regulations which would be made under the bill would not contain the proper safeguards to protect their rights. This is a justifiable misgiving, not only from the point of view of protecting the rights of Canadians who are manufacturing, whether they are small businessmen producing canned fruit or vegetables in Ontario or big conglomerates such as General Foods, but also because Canadian consumers will be affected by this bill. They have a right to know what these regulations will be. They have a right, either through consumers' associations or as individuals, to express their views on the proposed regulations to the minister and the government. If the minister does not accept my amendment, they will be denied that opportunity because the Canada Gazette does not have the widest possible circulation in Canada. As a matter of fact, the Canada Gazette is only read by politicians, senior civil servants and people who are directly involved in government at the federal, provincial and municipal levels.
What is wrong with the suggestion that the regulations be advertised in the leading newspaper of each province? This would give most people a chance to see what the government proposes to do with the power that Parliament will give it under this act. They will have this opportunity if the proposed regulations are advertised in the leading newspaper of each province. They will have an opportunity then to make their own recommendations known to the government, to protest to the government if that is necessary, or to indicate that the government has, in fact, not gone far enough to protect the consumer. I think it is worth noting that the total circulation of the Canada Gazette is less than 3,000. It has a very limited and exclusive readership which would not include the average consumer. Perhaps it might be worthwhile to place on the record a breakdown of the distribution of the Canada Gazette by provinces, in addition to the circulation of the leading newspapers in each of our 10 provinces.
In the province of British Columbia, the Canada Gazette enjoys a circulation of 114. Surely, the minister would want to have his regulations read by more people than the 114 in his province who read the Canada Gazette. I suggest to him that the way to do that would be to advertise the regulations in the Vancouver Sun, which has a circulation in excess of 210,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext: They would probably get it all wrong.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
In the province of Alberta, the Canada Gazette enjoys a circulation of 125, whereas the Edmonton Journal, the leading newspaper of that province, has a circulation of 147,000. In the province of Saskatchewan, the Canada Gazette has a circulation of 87, while the Regina Leader Post, the leading newspaper in that province, has a circulation of 60,000. In the province of Manitoba, the Canada Gazette has a circulation of 95, whereas the Winnipeg Free Press, the leading newspaper of that province, has a circulation of 130,000. In the province of Ontario, the Canada Gazette is a best seller by comparison. It enjoys a circulation of 1,362, whereas the Toronto Star, has a circulation of 400,000. In the province of Quebec, the Canada Gazette is not so popular. It has a circulation of 667, whereas the Montreal Star enjoys a circulation of 186,000, and La Presse in Montreal has a circulation of 206,000. In the province of New Brunswick, the Canada Gazette really takes a beating. It enjoys a circulation of 64, whereas the Saint John Telegraph-Journal has a circulation of 29,000. In the province of Nova Scotia, the Canada Gazette has a circulation of 69, whereas the Halifax Chronicle-Herald has a circulation of 68,000. In the province of Prince Edward Island, the Canada Gazette has a circulation of 11; that says something for Prince Edward Island. The Charlottetown Guardian enjoys a circulation of 16,500. In my own province of Newfoundland, the Canada Gazette has a circulation of 74, whereas the St. John's Evening Telegram enjoys a circulation of 46,000. When we get to Labrador, we find that the Canada Gazette has a circulation of only two.
I put these figures on the record to indicate to the House that the minister is defeating the very purpose of section 19 of the bill, which calls for the proposed regulations or amendments to a regulation to be advertised in the Canada Gazette. The reference is to regulations under section 11 of the bill which deals with undue proliferation, standardization, and so on. I ask the minister, is he serious about advertising these regulations, about having the widest dissemination of the regulations and encouraging the widest possible response to them? After all, he is not infallible, nor is the Governor in Council, and even though, hopefully, he will consult with consumer groups, with the Standards Council and with the trade groups, the proposed regulations will probably be lacking in many important aspects. There may be very serious shortcomings which would only be made known through the widest possible publication. It is obvious that they will not get this publicity unless my amendment is accepted.
Advertising in the Canada Gazette is merely a legal technicality. But surely in this particular bill, which comes close to being the minister's consumer's bill of rights and which will affect every single Canadian because we are all consumers, the minister should have departed from the standard, legalistic form of publishing the proposed regulations in the Canada Gazette. Perhaps he will be generous and accept our amendment since this is St. Patrick's Day and the minister may have a little Irish in him. There is some hope for the minister because his mother is Irish. Perhaps on St. Patrick's Day he might
March 17, 1971

be constrained to accept this amendment, knowing in his heart that it will improve this bill which is so dear to him. We all hope this measure will have the desired effect, since it is receiving the support of everyone in the House.
The principle of the bill is good, but the drafting is bad. It was necessary for the government to bring in a number of amendments. In so doing they incorporated many of the ideas that we had proposed. We had proposed eight amendments in the committee. I forget the number of amendments that were submitted by my colleagues in the NDP. Of our eight amendments, four eventually surfaced as government amendments, having been first rejected by the committee. We are pleased with that. We are pleased that we were able to improve the bill. The bill now before the House is a better bill than the one that received second reading last November. Great credit is due the minister that he saw the light and improved the bill. Now he can go one step further and accept this amendment, the purpose of which is to ensure that the people of this country will know exactly what their rights are with respect to this legislation. If there is one fault that the minister and his department have, it is that they bring in laws, amend the existing laws, and bring in new regulations, all of which are designed to protect the consumers across this country but the average consumer knows nothing about them. The minister himself admitted during discussion of his estimates the other day that he had only a very limited advertising budget.

I think his budget for advertising amendments to the Bills of Exchange Act was $15,000. This amount would not even be sufficient to let the people of my own province know that they have new rights with respect to bills of exchange and with respect to the sale of sales contracts to finance companies. Nobody in Canada knows about the amendments to the Bills of Exchange Act which every member in this House supported. I submit that nobody will know about this legislation. They will not be aware of the regulations which the Governor in Council will be empowered to set up under this bill unless these proposed regulations are first of all advertised widely right across the country. There is only one way to do that, and it is by advertising in the leading newspapers of each of the provinces. I made an offer to the minister, which I repeat here. If his budget is such that he cannot afford to advertise this important legislation, if he cannot give these important proposed regulations the publicity they deserve, then perhaps Parliament can find the money. I think it is important that we do so.
I think the minister should first accept the amendment, should agree with the argument that the proposed regulations should be as widely disseminated as possible, and then he can come back to Parliament. I am sure Parliament will vote him the necessary money. We believe this amendment would strengthen the bill, just as it has
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act
already been strengthened by previous amendments, many of them ours, albeit the government took credit for them. We believe this amendment is necessary if the people of Canada are to know of the rights they will enjoy under this legislation. We believe that the widest dissemination is necessary in order that these regulations will be honoured by people who are in the business of manufacturing, processing, packaging and distributing food and food products.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express briefly my support for the amendment. I support it on two bases. First, I think it is a very reasonable and just request that the consumers, the dealers and the processors should be advised of any regulations, or any amendments that are proposed to this new packaging bill. If it is as good as we think it is, why should we hesitate to tell the people about the bill, and about any changes or regulations that are going to be made?
My support for the amendment is also based on another part of this measure. I refer to clause 3(1) which has to do with the application of the bill. Here we have a piece of legislation drafted in such a way that we are incorporating in it one of the most dangerous principles I have ever heard in this House. I bring to the attention of hon. members this clause which reads:
-the provisions of this Act that by the terms of this Act or the regulations are applicable to any product apply notwithstanding any other Act or the Parliament of Canada.
This means that the bill and the regulations will take precedence over any other legislation that we have passed in this House. Who writes and draws up the regulations? Generally, it is public servants who draft regulations. Do you mean to tell me that we are going to allow regulations, drafted by public servants, to take precedence over any other act passed by this Parliament? This clause should not be in the bill.
I would not object if the clause read, "-by the terms of this Act are applicable to any product apply notwithstanding any other Act of the Parliament of Canada." If we allow the regulations made under the provisions of this bill to override any other act of Parliament, then we are creating a serious precedent. It is for this second reason in particular that I support the amendment. It would add weight to and strengthen the bill. If the bill is as good as we think it is, why not tell the people about the amendments and changes that will be made?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say briefly that we in the New Democratic Party support this amendment, but probably for somewhat different reasons from those given by our good friends to my right. First of all, I should tell the House that this amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is something of a compromise. It is different from the amendment that he originally moved in the committee. In order to make it easier on the minister, and to lessen the costs of his proposal, he is submitting a compromise amendment which would require the advertising of the regulations in one leading

March 17, 1971
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act newspaper in each province in Canada. I believe he means each territory as well.
I quite agree with what the hon. member said when he spoke to the amendment, namely, that the Canda Gazette is hardly a best seller, and that the subscribers to it in the main will be other government officials. I submit that the subscribers to the Canada Gazette will also be organizations, particularly those of the manufacturers, packagers and the processors of products which the consumers buy. No doubt these organizations subscribe to the Canada Gazette and watch it very closely. Certainly, their legal counsel will do the same thing. In addition, the consumers' associations subscribe to it. We support the amendment because we believe it is important that as many members of the general public as possible should have a chance to see the regulations and, if they wish, make representations.
Clause 19 of the bill requires the minister to publish the regulations in the Canada Gazette, and to afford an opportunity not only to the dealers and their associations but also to consumers to make representations regarding any regulations that are published. We feel that if the minister were at least to publish the regulations in one leading newspaper in each province, a significant number of members of the Canadian public would have a chance to look at them. Then, if they wished, they would have an opportunity to make representations. The argument that this will cost too much money surely is not sufficient to override the interests of the consumer. I know the minister is anxious that the public know as much about the bill as possible. Surely, this is one way in which that can be accomplished. I hope that the amendment will prove acceptable to him, since it does not in any way harm the legislation and does not in any way restrict or prevent him from carrying out all the provisions of the legislation. In fact, it will allow him to proceed even further in informing the general public about the regulations.
If the minister accepts the amendment, I hope that when his officials are preparing the advertisements for insertion in one leading newspaper in each province they see to it that the regulations are printed in a more attractive and readable manner than when they appear in the Canada Gazette. One becomes bored after reading the first line of the Canada Gazette. The regulations should be presented in an attractive form in a daily newspaper. Even if they had to be presented in the same way as a Safeway ad, this would be much better than if they appeared in the small type and legal verbiage associated with the Canada Gazette. I think the hon. member who has submitted the amendment has gone out of his way to reword his original proposal in such a manner as to make it more acceptable to the minister, with some saving of cost. I hope the minister will accept the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been urged to accept amendment No. 6 proposed by the hon. member for St.
John's East (Mr. McGrath). There is nothing I would like to do more than accept it, but I am afraid I cannot. I have been urged to accept it for two reasons, with both of which I agree. First, that today is St. Patrick's Day and the hon. member has some Irish blood as have I. My mother was born and brought up in Bandon and Cork, so on this day of the Irish I would like to agree with my friend from Newfoundland and accept this amendment but I am afraid I cannot. The second reason that I have been urged to accept is one with which I can also agree, that we should do everything possible to inform consumers of their rights. I agree with this, the hon. member for St. John's East agrees and so does the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). But this is not the most efficient or economical way of informing consumers, hence my objection to the amendment. The amendment is put forward in the best possible spirit in the world. I endorse that spirit, that desire which we all share to inform consumers of their rights.
As I explained in the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs where the bill was examined clause by clause, the cost of this proposal would be considerable. What the amendment calls for is the publication of the regulations passed under this act in the Canada Gazette and one leading newspaper in each province. Apart from the cost of publication in the Canada Gazette, the cost of publication in one newspaper would be extremely high. As an example the publication of the regulations passed under the Hazardous Products Act before Christmas relative to the safety of toys cost in excess of $15,000 for one publication. All that would be published in the legal column of a daily newspaper in one province would be some terribly complicated and legalistically worded regulation which no one would understand and we would spend $16,000 of taxpayers' money. And this would have to go on week after week as we proposed new regulations or amended and changed existing ones.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has a very limited budget. The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the budget in the committee on estimates recently when he supported the suggestion that we should have a larger budget for consumer education. I wish we had a larger budget but even so, this is not the way to spend it. What would be published would not be the regulations but only the proposed regulations. Unlike other acts of this Parliament except one, this act calls for publication of proposed regulations in the Canada Gazette. The bill states that the Governor in Council shall publish proposed regulations and allow people an opportunity to comment on them. At great cost to the taxpayers, all that would be published in the newspapers would be what we proposed to do. Various groups would then comment on them and suggest changes. We would then have to redraw the regulations and publish the final regulations. The amendment calls for publication of proposed regulations only, and this would cause great confusion. There is a better way than this to inform consumers of their rights.
This House has just completed debate on the statutory instruments' bill which arose from a special committee

March 17, 1971

which concerned itself with the whole question of delegated legislation, statutory instruments and the regulation-making power of the government and its agencies. In the published report of the special committee, a whole chapter is devoted to publication, but there is no suggestion of this type of procedure. The committee knew that there was a more efficient and economic way of informing the special interest groups and the general public of their rights, and the effect of regulations being passed, than is set out in this amendment. The special committee sat week after week and month after month studying this question of the regulation-making power of the government, and had they felt that this amendment was the right way to go about things we could take it for granted that it would have been included hi their recommendations. Because I think it would cause confusion, because the money spent would not be put to best use and because it has not been recommended by the special committee, I do not think the amendment can be accepted.
The government agrees with the spirit of the amendment of trying to inform consumers of their rights. However, we have already put into the bill a statutory requirement for the minister to publish proposed regulations. This requirement is contained in only one other act of this Parliament. In addition, there is a statutory duty on the minister to receive representations from all interested groups. That is a common statutory right which is usually taken for granted, but in this bill it is spelled out as a specific obligation.

speechtext:
Before starting to draw any regulation at all, we would notify the people known to be interested in whatever subject we were proposing to cover by way of regulation. For example, if we were dealing with toothpaste tubes or detergent packages or textile labelling, we would notify both the manufacturing and producer groups involved as well as the Consumers' Association of Canada. We would show them some general outline of our proposals and receive their comments, then we would draft regulations and submit them to the Department of Justice. Once they had been drawn and approved as the policy of the government, they would have to be published in the Canada Gazette as proposed regulations. However, long before publication those parties interested in the subject matter of the regulations would have been
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act
consulted and would have had an opportunity of making recommendations. Once published, of course, the statutory right to be heard arises. We would have to listen, and we would welcome comment on these regulations.
I think those who are interested in the regulations will experience no difficulty in knowing about them or in being heard. For example, the bill has arisen out of some 50 different recommendations of the Consumers Association of Canada. All of these were detailed recommendations, or detailed resolutions respecting some aspect of packaging and labelling. Most of these people are volunteers. This is not an expensive trade group, with high priced executives, directors, boards, and people who are paid to sit in the gallery of the House of Commons to ascertain what is happening. The Consumers Association is not like that. Nevertheless they, as volunteers, still are able to keep a watch on what is happening in my department, fortunately, and are able to make their input felt with respect to the making of regulations. They have done this effectively, and this bill provides the statutory right for them to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I did not reply to the hon. member's remarks because I thought they were out of order. They referred to clause 3, with which we are not now dealing. We are dealing with the amendment relating to the publication of regulations. We debated yesterday the provisions relating to clause 3. I quoted at that time from the debate in the committee. I commented on the brief from Dr. Ziegel, the prominent lawyer in this field in Canada, which suggests that clause 3 would not have the effect that the hon. member suggests it may have. Allow me to read clause 3(1):
Subject to subsection (2) and any regulations made under section 18, the provisions of this Act that by the terms of this Act or the regulations are applicable to any product apply notwithstanding any other Act of the Parliament of Canada.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the wording of clause 3(1) is clear. It provides that this act is the paramount act, and regulations made under this act are the paramount regulations. Since there are prior acts dealing with certain aspects of packaging and labelling, it is not unusual to provide in the latest act to come before Parliament, in this case the one we are considering, that that act and the regulations passed under it will govern and be paramount. That is the issue. That is what the bill provides. The substance of this bill is that this is the paramount legislation. This is to be the principal packaging and labelling legislation, and these are to be the principal regulations in this country. If you changed that, you would destroy the whole purpose of the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not our intention to delay this bill, since it has been around for almost four months. It was first introduced in the House on November 2 last year and received first reading, but did not come up for second reading until December 16. Since that time, Sir, it has received very exhaustive and intensive examination in committee. The Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs spent a total of 13 days examining this very important bill clause by clause, and heard 15 witnesses and as many briefs. That, coupled with the two days that the House has spent on report stage and third reading, means that the bill has received a total of 15 days debate and examination. And well it should, Sir, because it is an important bill. It is the most important consumer bill to come before this House. It certainly is the most important piece of consumer legislation to be introduced by this government.
The opposition has a responsibility in respect of government bills, and if the opposition supports the principle of a bill presented by the government it is then incumbent upon the opposition to examine that bill clause by clause, to submit amendments if necesssary, with the

March 17, 1971

intention of trying to improve the bill. Now, we have supported the principle of the bill. We have made this very clear throughout. When the bill first came up for second reading our intentions in this regard were made known, and our intentions were made known during the days when the bill was receiving clause by clause examination in the committee. Since we supported the principle of the bill, we felt that the bill needed improvements.
I think that the minister will be the first to admit that the bill which is now before the House is a vastly different piece of legislation from the one he originally introduced away back on November 2, 1970. It is a better bill. It is a better bill because members of the committee representing all parties examined it very closely clause by clause. It is a better bill because many of the amendments that we moved in committee, although rejected out of hand by the government by the use of its majority on the committee, eventually resurfaced as amendments proposed by government supporters at the instigation of the minister. So, we can take some credit for the fact that the bill now before the House is a vastly improved one. It is a better bill than the one that was originally introduced. Mr. Speaker, we believe that this was our responsibility and we have tried throughout to discharge that responsibility to the best of our ability.
The minister may try to convey the impression, sometimes supported by his colleagues from the NDP, that he is custodian of the rights of the consumer. He cannot say that to this party, Mr. Speaker. Every member of this House had very special responsibilities with regard to consumer rights and no party in this House has been as diligent and aggressive in discharging this responsibility as the official opposition.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, we take a back seat to no one, not the minister or his colleagues in the government or our well meaning and well inten-tioned friends in the NDP. In their more serious moments, I think hon. members in this House will concede this fact. However, we had very strong reservations and doubts about the way the bill was originally drafted. Indeed, we have doubts about some of the clauses of the bill in its present form.
One thing that causes us concern, Mr. Speaker, relates to the regulations which the minister will have the authority to draw under Clause 3. Reservations were expressed by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales). It is not that we have reason to doubt the minister's good intentions with respect to carrying out the intent of the bill; it is just that we do not believe the minister is the fountain of all knowledge and we do not believe that the Governor in Council is incapable of making mistakes. In view of the wide powers the minister will have under section 3 to draft regulations, which in some instances will supersede existing acts of Parliament, we believe the minister should give these proposed regulations the widest possible publicity. I submit to you, Sir, that it is not possible to do that under the
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act
present provisions of the bill. It is not possible to do that by publishing the proposed regulations in the Canada Gazette which has a very limited distribution, with a circulation of less than 3,000.
We believe that these regulations, which will be conceived by the Governor in Council after consultation with the consumers of Canada, with the Grocery Products Manufacturers' Association and other interested groups with the responsibility for manufacturing, packaging, distribution, will be presented in the Canada Gazette as proposed regulations. But we say because of the wide-ranging powers that the minister will or conceivably can have under these regulations, and because these regulations can supersede existing acts of this Parliament, they should receive the widest possible distribution so that consumer groups, co-operative groups and the average individual in this country who is concerned enough to express an opinion, can do just that. These interested parties should be able to criticize the regulations for their sins of omission or commission but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that they will be denied that opportunity because of the fact publication will be limited to the Canada Gazette.
There are 15 separate statutes presently in existence covering the packaging, labelling and, distribution of food and food products. They range all the way from the Weights and Measures Act, the Fish Inspection Act, the Meat and Canned Foods Act, to the Trademark and the Truth in Labelling Acts. The regulations which the minister has authority to draw up under clause 3 will supersede many of these 15 statutes. That is the concern of the opposition. It is our responsibility to be on guard against what would appear to be the excessive use of power by means of this use of statutory instruments. In other words, Parliament will have no say in the drafting of regulations. We say the people of Canada should have a chance to examine them before they are agreed upon and promulgated in final form. That was our main criticism of the bill
We support the bill in principle, Mr. Speaker. We have had our innings; we have submitted our amendments in committee and many of them were accepted by the government through the back door as government amendments. We submitted two of these amendments to the House because we felt that they focussed attention on our main concern, the drafting of the bill, notwithstanding what the minister said during debate and without detracting from the bill itself. The bill is ready for third reading and I want to make it clear that we are glad it has been improved by the amendments adopted in committee. It is a better bill because of them.
In supporting the bill, this party wants to reiterate and re-emphasize its position in support of some other protection in the area of packaging and labelling. There is no question that a case can be made for many of the powers which the minister would be receiving under the terms of this bill. There is undue proliferation in sizes and there is misleading labelling on many of the food items which appear on supermarket shelves. The case has been documented and I will not repeat it here. The minister was

March 17, 1971
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act co-chairman of a Special Joint Committee of the House and Senate on Consumer Credit which went into this problem in detail, and many of its recommendations are incorporated in this bill. The case has also been documented by the Royal Commission on Consumer Problems in the three Prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, under the chairmanship of Judge Mary Batten. The report of this commission is known as the Batten report.
We support the need for some protection. We want to emphasize and reiterate that support by supporting the bill on third reading.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we, too, approve this legislation as far as it goes, and I suppose the minister expected us to take that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext: Some day the hon. member may see the light.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
There are approximately 7,000 different prepackaged items at present on shop shelves in Canada. It is estimated that in the next four years there will be between 15,000 and 20,000 prepackaged items on the shop shelves of Canada. In other words, there will be a shoppers' jungle and it will be more difficult for shoppers to make intelligent decisions on the basis of quantity, quality and the value of the articles they purchase. Although I say this is a good bill as far as it goes, may I point out that we, of the New Democratic Party, took the minister at his word when he said in committee that we should worry less about the bill going too far and more about those areas in which the bill might not go far enough. In other words, he invited all hon. members to make certain that there are not areas in the bill that the minister and his officials missed or overlooked, to make sure that there are not loopholes which might be used to deceive or mislead, either intentionally or accidentally.
We took him at his word. We proposed a number of amendments in committee, none of which the minister would accept and all of which would have done even more than the minister proposed. In essence, he argued against the amendments, some of which he felt had merit, but he thought they were unconstitutional. In using that argument the minister is on extremely soft ground, because I submit, as we did earlier in this House and in committee, that if proposals we made to amend, strengthen and enlarge this bill were unconstitutional, then many other areas that the minister has included in this bill are also unconstitutional. For example, we think it is entirely illogical of the minister to require legislation that prevents deception in the area of sizes, shapes of packages or containers and contents on labels, while at the same time relying on the better nature and good ethical practices of those who manufacture, package, process and sell products to determine the matter of pricing. In dealing with the first three areas and ignoring the fourth, we think the minister is being illogical. However, we have half a loaf, and for a starving man that is better than none.
Because the minister has refused to accept amendments that would improve and enlarge the bill, we feel that within one or two years of its coming into operation he will find that some will utilize pricing practices to mislead or deceive, and that they will do this deliberately. Others will do this purely accidentally, but there will be no regulations under this legislation to correct that situation. We shall hear a further outcry from consumers once they become aware of those practices. We predict that after one or two years of experience with this legislation, the minister will regret having refused to accept our amendments regarding the storage and dating of perishable products. Such problems as we presently experience will not be corrected under this legislation.
As my hon. friend, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) pointed out, the committee heard witnesses from pretty well all organizations involved in the manufacture, packaging, labelling and processing of products. We also heard witnesses from the paper industry, most of whom opposed this legislation. There were a dozen or 15 of such associations appearing before the committee. On the other side of the coin, the Canadian Association of Consumers appeared before the committee in support of the legislation. I would hardly call that an even fight. Thank goodness, to the credit of the minister, as became evident in subsequent questioning, he lined himself up, in the main, on the side of the Canadian Association of Consumers and of consumers generally.
The Grocery Products Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Toilet Goods Manufacturers Association and the Paper and Packaging Manufacturing Association appeared before the committee and, I feel, deliberately exaggerated the intent and purpose of this legislation. In almost every instance, they read a great deal more into the legislation than is contained in it and said that the minister could do more than he can. They tried to mount a scare campaign. They were arrogant. They knew-they did not think-they knew that they knew better than anyone else what the needs, wishes and desires of consumers were. The president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association had the unmitigated gall to say in committee that they, the manufacturers, knew better than anybody else what the needs and desires of the consumers were. What conceit. What arrogance! I should like to think that the minister, as well as members of the committee, got the message loud and clear, because this kind of talk to a committee made up of representatives of the people of Canada should not be accepted.
We have seen more than one example of this kind of arrogance and conceit. The March issue of "Executive" carries a lengthy interview, if one can call it that so with Mr. John C. Lockwood, president of Lever Brothers Ltd. I never saw so many loaded questions in one interview in my life. The more one reads this interview the more one becomes incensed about it and the more becomes disappointed that the minister did not accept some of the amendments we proposed. I predict, in light of the attitude of this gentleman and others like him, that the minister will have a lot of fun, not to say difficulty, in
[Mr. McGrath.)
March 17, 1971

enforcing his law. He will find himself in court at almost every step of the way. There will be a fight over almost every regulation made.
In the article Mr. Lockwood is reported as saying:
The minister and his people think they know better than we do what the consumer wants, and that's an astonishing situation. After all we have spent years and hundreds of thousands of dollars in market research and have had tremendous exposure of our products to the marketplace.
That is perfectly true. Outfits like Lever Brothers have spent hundreds of thousands on market research and on exposing and selling their products. What is the reputation and history of companies which manufacture and peddle detergents and soaps? They introduce gimmickry, contests and prizes. Packages are partly filled. Packages contain a reduced amount of soap and in them is a tea towel worth less than one tenth of the value of the soap it displaces. Outfits like that have had to face courts because of the type of advertising they have carried on and because of the way they have presented their product to the public. This statement applies whether you are considering tooth paste, soap or what have you. These are the kinds of outfits that act in the manner characterized by Mr. Lockwood. He was asked this question in the interview:
Do you question whether this group of people know what they're doing; or do you question their motivation for doing it?
The group Mr. Lockwood refers to are, "The minister and his people-pseudo-intellectual characters," all of whom show a form of arrogance that has to be fought. Mr. Lockwood not only questions this group of people, not only questions what they are doing, but also questions their motivation for doing it. I hope that the minister will have an opportunity at some time to have a good discussion with Mr. Lockwood privately. I will even send over a pair of boxing gloves for him to use. Mr. Lockwood does not think they have the necessary data to work on because none of them have much experience with the consumer market and they tend to be influenced by a few letters addressed to Box 99 or a few intellectual friends.
As the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said, we spent dozens hours listening to gentlemen like Mr. Lockwood. People like him got a hearing in greater length and depth, I imagine, than they have ever received before. I shall not take the time of the House to go further into this article, but when we read it we realize what the minister and his department will be up against. If the minister thinks for one moment that he will receive co-operation, advice and help from this outfit he is labouring under a delusion. He can expect a lot more difficulty than he has envisaged so far and he will wish that more of the tools we were proposing for him in our amendments were available before another year is up. This gentleman, Mr. Lockwood, who represents the other side, uses phrases like "galloping Basfordism".

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Watch your language.
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think he gives the minister too much credit. Even the minister, good though his motives are, cannot claim credit for originating the ideas in this legislation. It seems to me expressions of this kind from outfits like Lever Brothers are symptomatic of their real attitude toward the public of Canada. Their attitude is-the public is ignorant, dumb, and a bunch of suckers. To quote the head of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the manufacturers know infinitely more. Such expressions are also symptomatic of their attitude toward Members of Parliament, including members of the other place who, in a joint committee which started this work in 1966, spent months listening to the outcries of consumers across the country; everyone in public life has for 15 years been subject to the complaints and distress of consumers by the tens of thousands. Mr. Lockwood would have us believe that he knows what the consumers want; that he and people like him have been pure in the marketplace; that they have never misled consumers; that their packages are designed to give the consumer a right to choose. But he never tells us what choice the consumer is given. I submit that too often it is a choice between which package or label he would be misled by.
I am glad to hear that the spokesman for the official opposition welcomes this legislation. One is tempted to be unkind, but I will resist that temptation for fear that third reading might not be forthcoming today.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
This has been a long road for the consumer and I will resist any temptation to say things about my friends in the official opposition. If I were to do so, I would have to go back a few years and quote prominent members of the Liberal party who did not think too much fuss need be made about consumer problems. They called people in the NDP and people in the Canadian Association of Consumers economic idiots, who were raising a tempest in a teapot. They concluded that these matters should be left to free enterprise, to the free market. But even they have become converted over the years.
To the minister's credit, his arrival and the arrival of some of his hon. friends in 1965 and later, speeded up this conversion. I hope that after a year or so of experience with this legislation the minister will come to this House with amendments when he finds-I did not say "if", but "when"-there are inadequacies which prevent him doing the job he wants to do. I hope he will not hesitate to persuade his colleagues that further enlargement of this legislation is necessary on the basis of his experience.
We are happy to see this legislation going through Parliament. We wish it went further in its provisions than it does, but we shall be glad to support it on third reading.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PROHIBITIONS, LABELS, STANDARDIZATION, INSPECTION, ETC.
speechtext:
If I might say a word before the debate on third reading is concluded, I should like to acknowledge

March 17, 1971
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act two speeches which have been made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on behalf of the Conservative party and by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). In acknowledging those speeches, I should like to thank the hon. members of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs who spent many days listening to a great range of witnesses from manufacturers associations, consumer organizations and the department in the course of examining the provisions of this bill. Some 23 sittings of the committee were held and the committee heard representations from 13 organizations in addition to hearing from myself and my officials. In addition, of course, the committee had to take account of numerous briefs and submissions from organizations which were not personally represented.
As the hon. member mentioned, a number of amendments were made in committee, including some important amendments. I acknowledge freely the germination of the ideas behind them; some of the points arose from ideas put forward by members of the opposition. I think the bill is a better bill today than it was when it went into committee, because of the suggestions by the government and the opposition, including the hon. member for St. John's East. I think that is not a criticism of me of the bill, or the government and the bill it introduced. Rather, it is to the credit of the parliamentary system and is an indication that Parliament is working. It also gives credit to the government and puts the lie to the allegation that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is always making that we are an arrogant government and do not care about the parliamentary process. As a matter of fact, I am delighted that the hon. member for St. John's East acknowledged that a number of amendments suggested by the official opposition had been accepted by me on behalf of the government. I think it is true that every bill I have introduced has been amended in committee. As I say, that is not a criticism of me or of my bills, but rather a credit to the parliamentary system and the operation of the democratic processes in this country.
I have mentioned this because we have now reached third reading stage and it has been indicated that the bill will have the unanimous support of every member of the House. I think this is significant in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre in, I think, amusing the House in describing the interview- which I must admit I have not seen-given by the president of Lever Bros., Mr. Lockwood, who was critical of what was going on in the consumer movement.
It seems to me that Mr. Lockwood and his colleagues should take note of the fact that the members of the House of Commons of Canada, duly elected from all parts of Canada, have considered this bill very carefully, have considered it in numerous hearings before its committee, have listened to briefs from manufacturing groups, producer groups and consumer groups, and as a result of all such deliberations have come to the conclusion that the bill is needed and should be supported
unanimously by Social Crediters, members of the New Democratic Party, members of the Conservative party and members of the government. If I were John Lockwood, the president of Lever Bros., or Colgate, I would consider this fact a pretty reliable consumer survey of what should be the law of this country. There are those in industry who support and are sympathetic to what the consumer movement is trying to do. I think those who do not fall into this category should take note of what is happening in this House this afternoon.
I also hope that those gentlemen in the other place who form the other part of this Parliament, and who sometimes have not been sympathetic to legislation introduced by the consumer affairs department will take note, not of editorials in the Financial Post or in the Financial Times, but of the fact that this bill is passing the House of Commons this afternoon, and passing unanimously. As a result, I trust they will treat this bill sympathetically when it arrives in the other place.
May I mention with your permission, Mr. Speaker, one other matter. In order to correct a misapprehension that has arisen, I would draw the attention of the House to the fact that in my statement on second reading, in raising the question of bilingual labelling, an error appears at page 2128 of Hansard for December 16, the third line from the bottom of the first column. I inadvertently omitted one line of my statement, and as a result some confusion has been caused with regard to bilingual labelling of imported products. At that time I was announcing that it was government policy to require, as a general practice, that consumer products that are subject to federal legislation be labelled in both official languages. Under the present practice some laws specify either one language or the other; some make no mention of language. Only the Hazardous Products Act and the Food and Drug Act specify labels in both languages.
As I was announcing in December, over the next few years all consumer products subject to federal legislation will progressively have to meet the bilingual labelling requirement, so that as quickly as practical and practicable bilingual labelling shall be mandatory at the point of manufacture. It is recognized that imports may require special attention to ensure that foreign suppliers are aware of the bilingual requirements. So, I want to emphasize that every effort will be made to encourage the earliest implementation of these new rules for imported products in order that they may conform, along with domestic products,-and that was the part left out of my earlier statement-to the five year target date that I announced in December. As I indicated, an interdepartmental committee will establish guidelines to ensure an orderly and efficient transition to this new policy.
I do not want to prolong the debate. I do once again want to thank hon. members for the attention and care they gave the bill during the course of debate both in the House and during the committee hearings. I am particularly grateful for the amendment made by the hon. member for St. John's East in the committee, as well as for those moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and Regina-Lake Centre.

March 17, 1971

I want to close by saying that some of the amendment suggested, particularly by New Democratic Party members, have been turned down by the House on my recommendation. The reason was I thought they jeopardized the constitutionality of the legislation. Although the members of the New Democratic Party said that that did not matter and that we should try them anyway, the very reason we should not draw legislation that may be attacked in the courts was emphasized today by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, who at two points in his discussion of the amendment mentioned he hoped that the minister would enforce the legislation; that he expected the minister would be in court a great deal with this legislation-I think they are his precise words. He also mentioned he hoped that the minister and the department knew what they would be up against when dealing with the private sector.
It is for the very reason that we do know what we will be up against in some instances, because we know that on occasion we will be in court, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said, because we do know there are people we will have to take to court in enforcing this legislation, that we have to draw legislation on the advice of the law officers of the Crown which is constitutional and will stand up in court. This is why we cannot accept some of the amendments that we would have accepted had we not received advice from the law officers of the Crown. As I say, there is no sense in drawing legislation
Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act
which at the first opportunity will be challenged in court and thrown out.
I conclude with those remarks. It merely remains for me to say that I hope the private sector will take note of the fact that the House of Commons of Canada has unanimously seen the need for the legislation and supported it. I also hope hon. gentlemen in the other place will take note of that fact.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
